implementation_notes: C++ blobs are easy to hide: `std::map` members and a dozen unrelated member variables make a class large without making it a blob, and a class can also be a god object. The blob-specific check is whether the members are related — if a method touches only three of forty fields and no other method touches those three, they are a candidate cluster. The C++-specific tooling is good here: clang-tidy reports class size and readability, and `include-what-you-use` plus the module graph show which members each method needs. Extraction into nested classes or free functions in the same namespace is the standard move.
idiom_name: fat class with unrelated members; partial classes as the usual disguise
pitfalls: A class holding a `std::map`/`std::vector` of containers is large without being a blob — the test is member cohesion, not member count.
A member of a container type makes the class appear to have one field while hiding hundreds, so size metrics under-report.
Nested classes extracted into the blob keep the outer class's coupling, so the blob's own header still grows.
